title: Nausea, vomiting, NG tubes and artificial nutrition
blurb: Confirm nasogastric tube position safely before every use, run enteral and parenteral feeds safely and manage nausea and vomiting.
question: Mrs Whitfield, 76, has a nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. Before her morning feed the nurse aspirates and tests the fluid: the pH is 6.5. She takes a proton pump inhibitor and looks comfortable. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: A nasogastric (NG) tube can pass into the airway instead of the oesophagus without obvious signs. Feeding, fluid or medicine given through a tube sitting in the lung or pleura can kill. A misplaced NG tube not detected before use is a Never Event: a serious incident that is wholly preventable when national safety guidance is followed. In plain English: no feed, flush or medicine goes down an NG tube until its position has been confirmed by an approved method.
teach.cite: NHS Improvement Patient Safety Alert (2016); NHS England Never Events list

teach.h: Aspirate pH and what it means
teach.caption: Empty stomach about pH 1–3, about 4–5 after food. Acid-reducing drugs can push gastric pH to 6 or more; healthy lung secretions are about pH 7.4 (HSSIB 2020, citing NHS Improvement 2016).

teach.h: Methods: use or do not use

rows.label: First line
values: pH of aspirate on CE-marked pH paper

rows.label: Second line
values: X-ray, reported by a competent person

teach.caption: NPSA 2005 and 2011 and NHS Improvement 2016 alerts: the whoosh test, litmus paper, the appearance of aspirate and absence of respiratory distress must not be used to confirm position. X-ray misinterpretation is the commonest single cause of NG Never Events.

teach.body: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement, and her proton pump inhibitor may explain the result, but the nurse cannot assume that. She does not feed, flush or give medicines. She follows local policy: check the external length mark, wait and retest, try repositioning her, and if the pH is still above 5.5 or there is no aspirate, seek a decision on X-ray confirmation. She documents each step.

Guidance
rows: Feed into the stomach unless upper GI dysfunction
Can be used 4 hours after insertion
Start at no more than 50% of needs for 24–48 h
Dedicated catheter or a dedicated lumen
teach.caption: NICE CG32 recs 1.7.6–1.7.10, 1.8.2, 1.8.8. Tubes are inserted only by staff with the relevant skills and training (1.7.16).

items: Assess: timing (before meals, after medicines), triggers, amount and appearance of vomit, and hydration.
Give prescribed antiemetics at the right time, for example before meals, and review whether they work.
Offer mouth care after vomiting; small, frequent meals; fresh air; remove strong smells.
Position a drowsy person on their side to protect the airway.
Record vomit volume on the fluid balance chart and escalate signs of dehydration or blood.

teach.h: If a fed person starts coughing or desaturating
teach.body: Coughing, breathlessness or falling oxygen saturation during an enteral feed suggest the tube may have moved or the person is aspirating. Stop the feed immediately, sit the person up, assess ABCDE and get urgent help. Do not restart until the tube position has been rechecked and the cause understood.
teach.cite: NICE CG32 rec 1.7.17; NHS Improvement 2016 alert

teach.text: The whoosh test is banned: hearing air bubble in the abdomen proves nothing, because sound can transmit from a tube in the lung. Litmus paper is also banned (use pH paper). And an X-ray is only safe if the person reading it is competent: misread X-rays are the commonest cause of NG Never Events.

items: Confirm NG position after placement and before each use (CG32 1.7.17).
First line: aspirate pH 5.5 or below on CE-marked pH paper; check external length mark.
pH above 5.5 or no aspirate: do not use; follow policy, X-ray if needed.
Never use the whoosh test, litmus, the look of aspirate or absence of distress.
Misplaced NG tube not detected before use = Never Event. Gastrostomy if feeding 4 weeks or more; PN via a dedicated line.

summary: You can now confirm nasogastric tube position before every use using pH and the external length, respond safely when the pH is above 5.5 or no aspirate is obtained, and apply NICE CG32 to enteral and parenteral nutrition. You can also give practical care for nausea and vomiting.

A.q: Mr Barker, 74, has had an NG tube inserted for feeding after a stroke. The nurse aspirates and tests the fluid on CE-marked pH paper. Which result confirms gastric placement?
options: pH 6.0 or below
pH 5.5 or below
pH 7.0 or above
pH 4.0 or above
A.why: NICE CG32 and the NHS Improvement 2016 alert: aspirate pH 5.5 or below (safe range 1–5.5) indicates gastric placement.

whyNot.0: pH 5.6–6.0 is above the safe cut-off and does not exclude respiratory placement.
whyNot.2: pH 7 or above is consistent with lung secretions.
whyNot.3: This range includes values above 5.5, which are not confirmatory.

A.q: Mr Patel, 83, has an NG tube that was confirmed in the stomach by X-ray yesterday. When should its position be checked again?
options: Once every 24 hours
After placement and before each use
Each time the feed bag is changed
When he shows signs of breathlessness
A.why: CG32 rec 1.7.17: confirm the position of all NG tubes after placement and before each use.

whyNot.0: Daily checks miss movement between uses.
whyNot.2: Bag changes are not the trigger; each use of the tube is.
whyNot.3: Waiting for breathlessness means harm may already have occurred.

A.q: A ward manager explains to staff which incidents count as Never Events. Which of these is one?
options: A feed running 30 minutes behind schedule
An NG tube pulled out by the patient overnight
An NG tube needing replacement after blocking
A misplaced NG tube not detected before use
A.why: NHS England's Never Events list includes a misplaced nasogastric or orogastric tube not detected before use.

whyNot.0: A delayed feed is an incident to address, not a Never Event.
whyNot.1: Accidental removal is common and not a Never Event.
whyNot.2: Tube replacement is routine care, not a Never Event.

B.q: Mrs Whitfield, 76, has an NG tube. Before her morning feed the aspirate pH is 6.5. She takes a proton pump inhibitor and is comfortable. What should the nurse do?
options: Start the feed, as the PPI explains the raised pH
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Inject air and listen over the stomach to confirm
Flush with 30 mL of water and start the feed slowly
B.why: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not use the tube; follow local policy (retest after waiting, reposition) and seek X-ray confirmation if needed (CG32 1.7.17).

whyNot.0: A PPI may raise pH, but placement still has to be confirmed before use.
whyNot.2: The whoosh test must not be used to confirm position.
whyNot.3: Flushing before confirmation is using an unconfirmed tube.

B.q: Mrs Hughes, 79, is receiving NG feed. She starts coughing, becomes breathless and her SpO2 falls from 96% to 89%. What should the nurse do first?
options: Slow the feed rate and recheck saturations in 15 minutes
Flush the tube with water to clear any blockage
Stop the feed, sit her up and call for urgent help
Aspirate the tube and check the pH before deciding
B.why: Coughing and desaturation during a feed suggest aspiration or a displaced tube: stop the feed, sit her up, assess ABCDE and get urgent help.

whyNot.0: Continuing the feed risks further aspiration.
whyNot.1: Flushing could push more fluid into the airway.
whyNot.3: Checking pH comes later; the emergency needs action first.

B.q: Mr Reid, 52, has short bowel syndrome and is starting parenteral nutrition through a multi-lumen central venous catheter. Which practice is consistent with NICE CG32?
options: Use a dedicated lumen for the parenteral nutrition
Give IV antibiotics through the same lumen as the PN
Start at full requirements on the first day
Take blood samples through the PN lumen
B.why: CG32 rec 1.8.8: a free dedicated lumen in a multi-lumen catheter may be used for PN; PN should start at no more than 50% of needs for 24–48 hours (1.8.2).

whyNot.1: Sharing the PN lumen increases infection and compatibility risk.
whyNot.2: CG32 starts PN at no more than 50% of estimated needs.
whyNot.3: Using the PN lumen for sampling breaches its dedicated use and raises infection risk.

C.q: Mrs Nolan, 70, has an NG tube. The nurse cannot obtain any aspirate despite turning her onto her side, waiting and trying again. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Inject 20 mL of air and listen for bubbling over the stomach
Start the feed at a low rate and observe her breathing closely
Follow local protocol and seek a decision on X-ray confirmation
Test the appearance of any fluid on the tip for a stomach colour
C.why: If no aspirate can be obtained after the recommended measures, the tube must not be used; follow local protocol, which includes X-ray confirmation by a competent person (CG32 1.7.17; NHS Improvement 2016).

whyNot.0: The whoosh test is unreliable and must not be used.
whyNot.1: Using an unconfirmed tube risks a Never Event.
whyNot.3: The appearance of aspirate must not be used to confirm position.

C.q: Mr Grant, 66, had a stroke 3 days ago and cannot swallow safely. The team expects he may need tube feeding for many months. What does NICE CG32 suggest?
options: Parenteral nutrition until his swallow returns
Thickened fluids by mouth alongside soft food
An NG trial now, then consider a gastrostomy
A gastrostomy straight away without NG feeding
C.why: CG32: after a stroke, people unable to swallow safely should have an initial 2–4 week NG trial; gastrostomy should be considered for those likely to need tube feeding for 4 weeks or more.

whyNot.0: His gut works, so enteral feeding is preferred over PN.
whyNot.1: Oral intake is unsafe until his swallow is assessed as safe.
whyNot.3: CG32 advises an initial NG trial in the acute stroke setting.

C.q: Mr Ellis, 61, is having chemotherapy and feels sick before every meal, leaving most of his food. He has a prescribed antiemetic that he takes after meals. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give the antiemetic before meals and review it
Ask the dietitian to start nasogastric feeding today
Encourage him to eat large meals when he feels hungry
Withhold food until his nausea has fully resolved
C.why: Timing the prescribed antiemetic before meals targets the nausea that stops him eating; reviewing its effect guides further changes with the prescriber.

whyNot.1: Tube feeding is a big step before simple measures have been tried.
whyNot.2: Small, frequent meals are usually better tolerated with nausea.
whyNot.3: Withholding food worsens his nutritional risk.

reteach.title: Prove it before you use it
reteach.question: Every use of an NG tube carries the same question: how do I know where the tip is right now?

blocks.body: The stomach is acidic; the lungs are not. So a small sample of fluid from the tube that turns CE-marked pH paper to 5.5 or below is evidence the tip is in the stomach. If you cannot get fluid, or the pH is higher, you have no evidence yet, so the tube stays unused until further checks (often an X-ray read by a competent person) give it. Sounds, colours and a calm patient are not evidence.

children.label: Do not use
children.sub: Reposition, wait, retry; X-ray if needed

blocks.text: A low pH confirms acid, not that the tip is in the stomach in every case; that is why the external length mark is checked too and why staff must be trained.

explain.body: After placement and before each use: before every feed, flush or medicine (CG32 1.7.17). If the external length mark has changed, the tube may have moved: do not use it until position is confirmed.

test.q: Which task needs NG tube position confirmed immediately beforehand?
options: Changing the bed linen around them
Giving a medicine via the tube
Recording a blood pressure
Cleaning the nostril area
test.why: CG32 rec 1.7.17: confirm NG position before each use, including every medicine, flush or feed.

whyNot.0: Linen changes do not put anything down the tube.
whyNot.2: Blood pressure measurement does not use the tube.
whyNot.3: Nasal care does not involve putting anything through the tube.

explain.body: Use CE-marked pH paper on gastric aspirate. Safe range pH 1–5.5. Above 5.5 or no aspirate: do not use; follow local policy. Acid-suppressing drugs can raise gastric pH.

items.label: upper limit of the safe pH range

test.q: Which product should be used to test NG aspirate?
options: Blue litmus paper
Urinalysis dipstick
CE-marked pH paper
Glucose test strip
test.why: National alerts require CE-marked pH paper; litmus must not be used.

whyNot.0: Litmus paper is banned for NG checks.
whyNot.1: Urine dipsticks are not designed or approved for aspirate pH.
whyNot.3: Glucose strips measure sugar, not pH.

explain.body: Do not use the whoosh test, litmus paper, the appearance of the aspirate or the absence of respiratory distress to confirm position. X-ray is second line and must be interpreted by a competent person.

test.q: Which method of confirming NG position is acceptable?
options: Listening for air bubbling
Checking aspirate looks gastric
Noting no coughing on insertion
Testing aspirate pH
test.why: Aspirate pH on CE-marked pH paper is the first-line method; X-ray is second line.

whyNot.1: Appearance of aspirate is unreliable and must not be used.
whyNot.2: Absence of respiratory distress does not exclude lung placement.

explain.body: Feed into the stomach unless upper GI dysfunction. Gastrostomy if 4 weeks or more. Stroke: 2–4 week NG trial. PEG usable 4 hours after uncomplicated insertion. PN: no more than 50% of needs for 24–48 hours, dedicated line or lumen.

test.q: Under NICE CG32, gastrostomy feeding should be considered for people likely to need tube feeding for at least how long?
options: 4 weeks
1 week
2 weeks
6 months
test.why: CG32 rec 1.7.8: consider gastrostomy for people likely to need long-term (4 weeks or more) enteral tube feeding.

whyNot.1: 1 week is short-term and usually managed by NG tube.
whyNot.2: 2 weeks is within the NG trial period after stroke.
whyNot.3: 6 months is far beyond the CG32 threshold.
